content: SIM1, also referred to as Single-minded homolog 1 or class E basic helix-loop-helix protein 14 (bHLHe14), is a protein encoded by the SIM1 gene in humans. The SIM1 and SIM2 genes are homologs of the Drosophila melanogaster single-minded (sim) gene. The name single-minded originates from the observation that, in sim mutant embryos, cells located at the midline fail to develop properly and eventually die. This results in the collapse of the paired longitudinal axon bundles, which normally span the anterior-posterior axis of the embryo (analogous to the spinal cord in humans), into a single rudimentary axon bundle at the midline. The sim gene encodes a basic helix-loop-helix-PAS domain transcription factor that regulates gene expression in midline cells. Given the critical role of the sim gene in Drosophila development and its peak expression during neurogenesis, it has been hypothesized that the human SIM2 gene, located in a critical region of chromosome 21, may contribute to certain dysmorphic features (particularly facial and skull characteristics), brain development abnormalities, and/or intellectual disabilities associated with Down syndrome. Additionally, SIM2 has been implicated in causing a Prader-Willi-like phenotype in other cases. Studies in mice have demonstrated that haploinsufficiency of Sim1 leads to obesity caused by hyperphagia (excessive eating) and an inability to properly respond to increased dietary fat. Conversely, overexpression of SIM1 has been shown to protect against diet-induced obesity and to rescue the hyperphagia observed in agouti yellow mice, which have disrupted melanocortin signaling. The obesity and hyperphagia observed in these cases may be mediated by impaired melanocortin activation of paraventricular nucleus (PVN) neurons and a deficiency in oxytocin production. It has also been shown that postnatal modulation of Sim1 levels results in hyperphagia and obesity, indicating that SIM1 has a physiological role beyond its developmental functions. In terms of molecular interactions, SIM1 has been demonstrated to interact with the aryl hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator (ARNT).
